abstract: We propose Any2graph, a generic framework for end-to-end Supervised Graph Prediction (SGP) i.e. a deep learning model that predicts an entire graph for any kind of input. The framework is built on a novel Optimal Transport loss, the Partially-Masked Fused Gromov-Wasserstein, that exhibits all necessary properties (permutation invariance, differentiability and scalability) and is designed to handle any-sized graphs. Numerical experiments showcase the versatility of the approach that outperform existing competitors on a novel challenging synthetic dataset and a variety of real-world tasks such as map construction from satellite image (Sat2Graph) or molecule prediction from fingerprint (Fingerprint2Graph).

summary.idea: Any2Graph uses an optimal-transport loss that matches graph structure and features while handling partially masked predictions. The loss is designed for permutation invariance, differentiability, and scalability.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not report graph sizes, runtime, or task-specific accuracy. Its generic framework is demonstrated on selected input types; the title's broad scope does not establish equal performance on every possible graph-prediction problem.
summary.problem: Predicting an entire graph is difficult because graphs vary in size and node order has no intrinsic meaning. A training loss must compare structures without depending on arbitrary indexing.
summary.results: Experiments outperform compared methods on a challenging synthetic dataset and real tasks including map construction from satellite imagery and molecular graph prediction from fingerprints.
summary.tldr: Train graph prediction end to end with a loss that compares structure independently of node ordering.

title: Any2Graph: Deep End-To-End Supervised Graph Prediction With An Optimal Transport Loss

abstract: Time series forecasting plays a pivotal role in various real-world applications and has attracted significant attention in recent decades. While recent methods have achieved remarkable accuracy by incorporating advanced inductive biases and training strategies, we observe that instance-level variations remain a significant challenge. These variations—stemming from distribution shifts, missing data, and long-tail patterns—often lead to suboptimal forecasts for specific instances, even when overall performance appears strong. To address this issue, we propose a model-agnostic framework, PIR, designed to enhance forecasting performance through Post-forecasting Identification and Revision. Specifically, PIR first identifies biased forecast instances by estimating their predictive accuracy. Based on this, the framework revises the forecasts using contextual information, including covariates and historical time series, from both local and global perspectives in a post-processing fashion. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets with mainstream forecasting models demonstrate that PIR effectively mitigates instance-level errors and significantly improves forecasting reliability.
title: Improving Time Series Forecasting via Instance-aware Post-hoc Revision
